name: Pink Quill
description: A unique member of the Tillandsia family, Pink Quill is actually a terrestrial bromeliad that prefers to grow potted rather than mounted like typical air plants. Native to Ecuador, it produces one of the most spectacular flowering displays in the bromeliad world: a large, flattened pink paddle-shaped bract that can last for months, with vibrant purple-blue flowers emerging sequentially along its edges. The plant forms an attractive rosette of narrow, arching green leaves that can reach 10-12 inches tall. Unlike true epiphytic air plants, Pink Quill thrives best when planted in a well-draining orchid or bark mix, making it an excellent choice for those who prefer traditional potted plants with extraordinary blooms.
toxicity: Pet safety unknown — not listed by the ASPCA, and we found no reports of it being toxic.
careInstructions: Keep the potting mix lightly moist but never soggy - let excess water drain away
Mist leaves 2-3 times per week to maintain humidity
Or grow it mounted like an air plant: from spring to autumn, immerse it in rainwater twice a week, drain well and let it dry
Plant in a free-draining mix of fine bark or orchid compost with grit or perlite
Provide bright, filtered light - avoid direct sun which can scorch leaves
Maintain moderate to high humidity for best flowering
The pink bract lasts for months; once it fades, cut it off - each rosette flowers only once
After main bloom spike fades, plant will produce offsets (pups) before dying
Feed monthly from spring to autumn at quarter strength - a bromeliad fertilizer, or a foliar mist of balanced feed
commonProblems: Brown leaf tips: Low humidity, water quality issues, or fluoride sensitivity
Fading flower spike: Natural after several months of blooming
Root rot: Overwatering or poorly draining potting mix
No blooming: Insufficient bright light, plant too young, or needs maturity (2-3 years)
Yellowing leaves: Overwatering or natural die-back after flowering cycle completes

fertilizing.fertilizerType: Bromeliad fertilizer or foliar balanced feed at quarter strength
fertilizing.tip: Feed monthly from spring to autumn at quarter strength - a bromeliad fertilizer, or a foliar mist of balanced feed

repotting.tip: Pot it in a free-draining bromeliad mix; it needs only enough mix to hold it steady.
repotting.soil: Fine bark or orchid compost, grit and coir in equal parts

whatsNormal: Each rosette flowers once: the bract lasts for months, then the rosette slowly dies while pups grow around its base.
Soft-leaved air plants like this one want more moisture and less light than the silvery, hard-leaved kinds.
Its newer botanical name is Wallisia cyanea.

propagation.tip: Separate pups once they are at least a third the size of the parent.

flags.note: Toxicity: no pet rating from ASPCA, NC State or the University of California — shown as "unknown". ASPCA rates several other bromeliad genera non-toxic (Neoregelia, Guzmania, Cryptanthus) but none in Tillandsia or Wallisia, so it stays "unknown".

Two growing methods: Clemson describes it as a terrestrial species that "needs moist soil" (the potted plant usually sold); RHS grows it mounted with no compost, immersed in rainwater twice a week. Care text leads with potted and offers the mounted method as an alternative.
Winter watering (5 days) is our estimate — RHS says water bromeliads more sparingly in winter.
Temperature, humidity and feeding come from bromeliad-wide guidance (RHS, Wisconsin, Clemson), not a page for this species.

Watering "when the top inch is dry" → keep lightly moist (Clemson, RHS); "remove spent flowers to encourage continued blooming" → each rosette flowers once (RHS); feeding now quarter strength, monthly spring to autumn.
